SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vaginosis (SH f:
What & Why — the GUM-Clinic Angle

In a sexual health setting, BV matters for a slightly different reason than in gynaecology. It’s the single commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge presenting to GUM, and the clinician’s first job is to place it correctly on the STI-vs-not-STI map: BV is NOT a sexually transmitted infection, but it is sexually associated (more common with new/multiple partners + unprotected sex) and, crucially, it increases susceptibility to acquiring true STIs, including HIV. About half of women with BV have no symptoms, and it often resolves on its own — which is why an incidental finding on a routine swab does not automatically need antibiotics.

So in GUM, BV is both a discharge to diagnose and treat and a flag that prompts full STI screening.
The mechanism (unchanged): loss of protective lactobacilli → vaginal pH rises above 4.5 → overgrowth of anaerobes (chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis). Everything flows from that loss of acidity. (See the Obs & Gynae “Pelvic & Vaginal Infections” note for the full clinical work-up.)
The Decisive Fork (SH version) — STI, or Not?

In GUM the discharge differential is framed explicitly by transmissibility — because it dictates partner notification:

The GUM teaching point: BV and trichomoniasis look similar (both raise pH, both can smell fishy), but only trichomoniasis triggers partner notification + contact tracing. Getting the STI/not-STI call right is the whole reason for accurate diagnosis here.
Sexual-Risk Associations (the SH emphasis)
  • More common with a new sexual partner, multiple partners, and unprotected sex — though it also occurs in women who’ve never been sexually active (hence “associated”, not “transmitted”)
  • Receptive oral sex, douching, and some hygiene practices disturb the flora
  • Increases the risk of acquiring STIs including HIV (raised pH + loss of the lactobacillus barrier), and increases onward HIV transmission risk
  • Associated with PID and endometrial infection, and with post-procedural infection (e.g. after termination of pregnancy or IUD insertion) — which is why BV found before such a procedure is treated even if asymptomatic
Diagnosis — Amsel’s Criteria (≥3 of 4)
📷 Image placeholder — Wet-mount microscopy showing clue cells — vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent coccobacilli giving a stippled, blurred border (a positive Amsel/Hay-Ison finding).
  • Thin, white, homogenous discharge
  • Vaginal pH >4.5
  • Clue cells on microscopy
  • Positive whiff/amine test (fishy odour with KOH)
In GUM this is done at the point of care with narrow-range pH paper + microscopy of a wet and Gram-stained slide. The Gram film is graded by Hay-Ison: grade I = lactobacilli only (normal), grade II = intermediate mixed flora, grade III = BV (few or no lactobacilli, mixed morphotypes). Nugent scoring is the equivalent numerical system (7–10 = BV), used mainly in research and laboratory settings.
pH pitfalls: blood, semen, lubricant and cervical mucus all push the reading up. Sample from the lateral vaginal wall, not the cervix or the pool of discharge — and never diagnose on pH alone, it is one of four criteria.
Management — with the SH Additions (BASHH)
  • Asymptomatic BV usually needs no treatment — it often resolves spontaneously. Do treat if BV is found before a procedure such as termination of pregnancy or IUD insertion. Pregnancy is NOT an indication to screen for, or routinely treat, asymptomatic BV — doing so does not reduce preterm birth (NICE)
  • First-line: oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days
  • Alternatives: metronidazole 2 g single oral dose (better adherence, slightly higher relapse; not in pregnancy or breastfeeding); intravaginal metronidazole 0.75% gel, one applicator at night for 5 nights; or intravaginal clindamycin 2% cream, one applicator at night for 7 nights
  • Advice: avoid douching, and washing with soap, shower gel, bubble bath, antiseptics or bath additives — wash the vulva with water or a plain emollient only. This is the key preventive measure and the first thing to address in recurrence
Two prescribing warnings you must give: (1) Clindamycin cream is oil-based and damages latex condoms and diaphragms — they cannot be relied on during treatment and for at least 5 days afterwards, so warn about both contraceptive failure and loss of STI protection (BNF). (2) Metronidazole and alcohol — advise avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours afterwards. A disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting) is the classical teaching; the strength of the interaction has been questioned, but “avoid alcohol” remains the advice to give (BNF).
🔬 SH-specific — screen
  • Offer a full STI screen — BV is a marker of sexual-risk exposure + frequently co-exists with STIs
  • Test for chlamydia + gonorrhoea (NAAT), trichomonas, and offer HIV + syphilis serology
👥 SH-specific — partners
  • Do NOT routinely treat male partners, and BV does not trigger partner notification or contact tracing — the key contrast with true-STI management
  • Female partners: BV is more concordant in women who have sex with women — consider assessment, though routine partner treatment still isn’t recommended
Recurrence is common (over half within a year) — address modifiable factors; suppressive regimens for frequent recurrence.
Pregnancy: BV is associated with late (second-trimester) miscarriage, preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight and postpartum endometritis. Treat symptomatic BV for symptom relief — oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days; avoid the 2 g single dose in pregnancy and in breastfeeding (BNF). Treating BV has not been shown to reduce preterm birth, which is why asymptomatic pregnant women are neither screened nor routinely treated (NICE).
Exam Pearls (SH-oriented)
What it is
Commonest cause of abnormal discharge; NOT an STI but sexually ASSOCIATED (new/multiple partners, unprotected sex).
Why it matters in GUM
Increases risk of acquiring STIs including HIV.
Discharge
Thin white FISHY, pH >4.5, no itch — vs trichomonas (STI, frothy green) and candida (not STI, itchy, pH <4.5).
Amsel’s (≥3 of 4)
Thin discharge + pH >4.5 + clue cells + positive whiff. Point-of-care pH + microscopy in GUM.
1st-line
Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD 5–7 days. Avoid alcohol during and for 48 h after. Avoid douching/vaginal soaps. Clindamycin cream damages latex condoms.
SH management
Full STI screen (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT, trichomonas, HIV, syphilis) — but no routine partner treatment and no partner notification (unlike true STIs).
Recurrence / pregnancy
Recurrence common (over half within a year). In pregnancy treat SYMPTOMATIC BV for symptoms — metronidazole 400 mg BD 5–7 days, not the 2 g dose. Do NOT screen or treat asymptomatic BV: it does not reduce preterm birth.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (genital):
What & Why

Vaginal candidiasis (“thrush”) is a symptomatic fungal infection of the vulva and vagina, usually caused by the yeast Candida. It’s extremely common (most women have at least one episode), it’s the itchy, non-STI member of the vaginal-discharge trio (the key contrast with BV and trichomonas), and recurrent disease has its own examinable management + prompts a search for an underlying cause (diabetes).

The organism & concept: ~80% Candida albicans. Candida can colonise the vagina asymptomatically and only cause infection when the local balance shifts — which is why the risk factors are all states that disturb flora or immunity.
The Decisive Fork — Candida vs BV vs Trichomonas

Thrush is the itchy, normal-pH, not-an-STI one — the pH is the cleanest discriminator:

CauseYeast (not STI)Anaerobes (not STI)Protozoan (STI)
DischargeThick, white, “cottage cheese”Thin, white/greyFrothy, yellow-green
OdourNon-offensiveFishyOffensive
pH<4.5 (NORMAL)>4.5>4.5
ItchProminentMinimalYes
Partner Rx?No (unless symptomatic)NoYes
Risk Factors (anything disturbing flora/immunity)
  • Diabetes mellitus (especially poorly controlled)
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (wipe out protective bacteria)
  • Pregnancy (high oestrogen)
  • Immunosuppression (steroids, HIV, chemotherapy)
  • High oestrogen states; sometimes the COCP
  • Oestrogen-dependent — uncommon before puberty and after the menopause unless on HRT, diabetic or immunosuppressed. Thrush in a postmenopausal woman should prompt a hard look for lichen sclerosus, vulval atrophy or undiagnosed diabetes
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Vulvovaginal candidiasis — thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge with vulval erythema, fissuring and satellite lesions.
  • “Cottage cheese”, thick, non-offensive white discharge
  • Vulval itch and irritation (the dominant symptom)
  • Vulvitis: superficial dyspareunia, dysuria (external, from inflamed vulva)
  • Vulval erythema, fissuring, and satellite lesions on examination
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Wet-mount/KOH microscopy showing Candida budding yeasts and pseudohyphae (HVS reserved for recurrent/atypical/treatment-failure cases).
  • A high vaginal swab is NOT routinely needed if the picture is typical — diagnose clinically and treat
  • Vaginal pH — the key bedside test: candida pH <4.5 (normal) vs BV/trichomonas pH >4.5
  • HVS for microscopy/culture (MCS) — reserved for recurrent, atypical, or treatment-failure cases (identifies non-albicans species, e.g. C. glabrata)
  • Candida is a common incidental finding on cervical screening cytology or a swab — around 1 in 5 women are colonised asymptomatically. Cytology is not the diagnostic test, and asymptomatic candida is NOT treated: treat symptoms, not swab or smear results
Management (BASHH/NICE)
💊 Uncomplicated (non-pregnant)
  • Two equally effective options — choose by patient preference and contraindications:
  • Oral: fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose — not in pregnancy; check interactions (it raises the INR with warfarin and raises statin levels)
  • Intravaginal: clotrimazole 500 mg pessary (single dose) — used when oral is contraindicated or not wanted
  • If vulval symptoms → add a topical imidazole cream (clotrimazole) to the vulva
  • Severe symptoms (extensive erythema, fissuring, excoriation) → give a second dose 72 hours after the first (fluconazole 150 mg, or a repeat clotrimazole 500 mg pessary)
  • Warn: imidazole creams and pessaries damage latex condoms and diaphragms — they cannot be relied on during treatment and for at least 5 days afterwards; polyurethane condoms are unaffected
  • Self-care: use a soap substitute or emollient wash instead of soap and shower gel; avoid perfumed products, vaginal deodorants, wipes and douching; avoid over-washing
🤰 Pregnancy
  • Do NOT use oral fluconazole — first-trimester exposure has been linked to miscarriage and congenital abnormalities
  • Topical only — an intravaginal imidazole (clotrimazole) pessary or cream, given as a longer 7-night course (not a single dose), because cure rates with single-dose topical treatment are lower in pregnancy
Recurrent candidiasis (≥4 symptomatic episodes in 12 months, at least 2 confirmed)
  • Check compliance with previous treatment
  • Confirm the diagnosis microbiologically: at least 2 of the episodes must be confirmed on microscopy or culture — self-reported episodes alone are not enough. HVS for MCS also identifies the species and sensitivities
  • Look for an underlying cause: blood glucose / HbA1c for diabetes (the key one); review recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and corticosteroids; consider immunosuppression, and offer an HIV test if the disease is severe, unexplained or there are other risk factors
  • Exclude differentials — e.g. lichen sclerosus, contact/irritant dermatitis, other causes of vulval itch
  • If a non-albicans species is grown (e.g. C. glabrata): standard azoles are often ineffective — discuss with or refer to sexual health services
Induction–maintenance regimen: Induction — oral fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses (days 1, 4, 7). Maintenance — oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months. Advice: avoid vaginal irritants (soaps, shower gels, wipes, douching) and use a soap substitute.
Not everything itchy is thrush. If there is itch without abnormal discharge, or antifungals repeatedly fail, think non-infective causes: contact/irritant dermatitis (diffuse erythema, soreness and stinging, often provoked by soaps, wipes, panty liners or the antifungal creams themselves); lichen sclerosus (white, atrophic, “porcelain” plaques in a figure-of-eight vulval/perianal distribution with loss of the labia minora — needs a potent topical steroid, not an antifungal); and genitourinary syndrome of the menopause (dryness and soreness with a pale, atrophic vagina).
Partners: candidiasis is not sexually transmitted, so partners are not routinely treated or notified and treating an asymptomatic partner does not reduce recurrence. A partner who is themselves symptomatic — most often candidal balanitis in a male partner (itchy, sore, red glans with small papules or satellite lesions, sometimes a subpreputial white discharge) — should be examined and treated in their own right, with topical clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily until symptoms settle, saline washing and a soap substitute. Recurrent or florid balanitis should prompt a glucose/HbA1c check, and persistent balanitis that fails antifungals needs a specialist opinion.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Symptomatic Candida (80% C. albicans); NOT an STI; the itchy, normal-pH member of the discharge trio.
Discharge
Thick, white, “cottage cheese”, non-offensive + vulval itch; pH <4.5 (NORMAL) — the key discriminator from BV/trichomonas.
Risk factors
Diabetes, antibiotics, pregnancy, immunosuppression, high oestrogen.
Diagnosis
Diagnose clinically → no routine swab (swab only if recurrent/atypical/treatment failure).
1st-line
Oral fluconazole 150 mg stat OR clotrimazole 500 mg pessary — equal efficacy, patient choice. Add a topical azole for vulval symptoms. Fluconazole: avoid in pregnancy; interacts with warfarin and statins.
Pregnancy
NO oral fluconazole → topical imidazole only, as a longer 7-night course rather than a single dose.
Recurrent (≥4/yr, ≥2 confirmed)
Confirm microbiologically (HVS + glucose/HbA1c), exclude dermatitis and lichen sclerosus, then induction (fluconazole 150 mg every 72 h ×3) + maintenance (150 mg weekly ×6 months).
Partners
Not sexually transmitted → no routine partner treatment; treat a partner only if symptomatic (e.g. candidal balanitis).
SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia:
What & Why

Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis — the commonest STI in the UK. It’s mostly asymptomatic (so it spreads silently → the target of a national screening programme), and untreated infection causes serious reproductive complications — PID, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal infertility in women, epididymo-orchitis in men.

The organism: Chlamydia trachomatis — an obligate intracellular bacterium (it has a gram-negative-like envelope but is atypical and doesn’t Gram-stain well). Serovars D–K cause genital infection; L1–L3 cause LGV.
The National Chlamydia Screening Programme (NCSP)
  • In England, opportunistic screening is offered to women and people with a cervix aged 15–24 — annually, or on change of sexual partner (UKHSA)
  • Asymptomatic young men are no longer offered opportunistic screening outside sexual health services — they are still tested if symptomatic, if they ask at a sexual health service, or as a partner of a case
  • Anyone under 25 who tests positive is re-tested about 3 months after treatment — this detects re-infection, NOT a test of cure (treatment is highly effective)
  • Standard GUM STI screen checks: Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea, Syphilis (blood), HIV (blood)
Clinical Features
Most cases are asymptomatic (~70% of women, ~50% of men) — the reason for screening.
WomenMenOn examination
Abnormal vaginal dischargeUrethral discharge/discomfortPelvic/abdominal tenderness
Pelvic painDysuriaCervical motion tenderness (excitation)
Abnormal bleeding (IMB/PCB)Epididymo-orchitisInflamed cervix, contact bleeding
Deep dyspareunia; dysuriaReactive arthritis (both sexes, commoner in men)Purulent/mucopurulent discharge
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — First-line NAAT specimens — self-taken vulvovaginal swab (women) vs first-catch urine (men); add rectal/pharyngeal swabs by exposure.
  • Diagnosis by NAAT — highly sensitive/specific
  • First-line in women: vulvovaginal swab (self-taken is fine)
  • First-line in men: first-catch urine
  • Other sites by exposure: urethral, rectal swab (anal sex), pharyngeal swab (oral sex)
  • Test at all sites of potential exposure; offer a full STI screen
  • Window period ~2 weeks: a NAAT taken within 2 weeks of the last exposure may be falsely negative — repeat it 2 weeks after exposure, and consider treating empirically if the contact was a known case
Management (BASHH)
First-line (uncomplicated): doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (for urogenital, rectal + pharyngeal infection). Counsel: swallow with plenty of water sitting or standing upright, avoid strong sun and sunbeds (photosensitivity), and do not use in pregnancy or breastfeeding (BNF).
What changed: the single 1 g azithromycin dose has been removed as a routine alternative — doxycycline is now clearly preferred (higher cure rates, especially for rectal infection and against co-existing Mycoplasma genitalium).
🤰 If doxycycline contraindicated (pregnancy, breastfeeding, tetracycline allergy)
  • Azithromycin 1 g stat, then 500 mg OD for 2 days (the 3-day regimen) — the usual choice in pregnancy, after a benefit/risk discussion, particularly in the first trimester
  • Erythromycin 500 mg QDS for 7 days, or amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days
  • In pregnancy, always arrange a test of cure
🔁 Test of cure (TOC)
  • Not routinely needed — treatment is highly effective
  • Do one in: pregnancy; rectal infection; persistent symptoms; or suspected poor adherence or re-exposure
  • Defer it to at least 3 weeks after finishing treatment — a NAAT can stay positive for 3–5 weeks from dead organisms
General advice: no sex (including oral) until the course is finished — 7 days for standard doxycycline, or 7 days from a short-course regimen — and until all partners have completed treatment. Refer to GUM for contact tracing / partner notification: look back 4 weeks before symptom onset for men with symptomatic urethral infection, and 6 months (or to the last sexual partner, if longer ago) for everyone else. Test for other STIs.
Complications
♀️ Women
  • PID → chronic pelvic pain, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy
  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis — perihepatitis (RUQ pain + adhesions)
  • Pregnancy/neonatal: ectopic, preterm birth, PROM, low birth weight, postpartum endometritis; neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) + pneumonia (vertical transmission)
♂️ Men / both
  • Epididymo-orchitis
  • Reactive arthritis — “can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree” (conjunctivitis, urethritis, arthritis) — chlamydia is the classic trigger
  • Chlamydial conjunctivitis (autoinoculation)
Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)
📷 Image placeholder — LGV progression — transient painless ulcer/papule → painful inguinal buboes or proctocolitis (mimics IBD in MSM) → late strictures/fistulae; treat with 21 days doxycycline.

A chlamydial infection (serovars L1–L3) affecting lymphoid tissue; increasingly seen in MSM, often with HIV co-infection.

  • Primary: a small, transient painless genital/rectal ulcer or papule
  • Secondary — inguinal syndrome: painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (“buboes”) / lymphadenitis
  • Secondary — anorectal syndrome: proctocolitis — change in bowel habit, anal pain, tenesmus, discharge (can mimic IBD in MSM); this is the usual UK presentation
  • Late (tertiary), if untreated: rectal strictures and fistulae, and genital lymphoedema
Management: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days (longer course than uncomplicated chlamydia); erythromycin/azithromycin are alternatives.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Chlamydia trachomatis = commonest UK STI; obligate intracellular; mostly ASYMPTOMATIC.
NCSP
Opportunistic screening = women/people with a cervix aged 15–24, annually or on partner change (men only if symptomatic, on request, or as contacts); re-test positives at 3 months for re-infection, not cure.
Diagnose
NAAT: vulvovaginal swab (women), first-catch urine (men); + rectal/pharyngeal by exposure.
1st-line
Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days. (Single-dose azithromycin removed as routine option.)
Pregnancy/allergy
Azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg OD ×2 days, or erythromycin/amoxicillin. Always TOC in pregnancy.
TOC
Not routine — do in pregnancy, rectal infection, persistent symptoms, or poor adherence/re-exposure; at least 3 weeks after finishing treatment.
Advice
No sex until the course is finished (7 days) and until partners are treated; GUM referral for contact tracing — 4 weeks before symptom onset for symptomatic urethral infection in men, otherwise 6 months.
Complications
PID → ectopic/infertility, epididymo-orchitis, reactive arthritis (can’t see/pee/climb), neonatal conjunctivitis & pneumonia, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis.
LGV
Serovars L1–L3, MSM: painless ulcer → buboes or proctocolitis (both secondary) → late strictures/fistulae; doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orchitis:
What & Why

Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis (± the testis) — pain, swelling and inflammation triggered by infection. It’s a common cause of acute scrotal pain, and — critically — its key differential is testicular torsion, a surgical emergency that must be excluded urgently in younger men before you settle on this diagnosis.

The examinable essence: exclude torsion, work out the likely organism from sexual history and risk factors, and treat accordingly. Age is a guide, not a rule — a man over 35 who is sexually active can still have a chlamydial or gonococcal cause, and a young man with a catheter or recent instrumentation can have an enteric one.
The Decisive Fork — STI or Enteric Organism? (age & sexual history)
📷 Image placeholder — Age/sexual-history flowchart — <35 sexually active → chlamydia/gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 1g + doxycycline); >35 / catheter / UTI → E. coli enteric (ofloxacin).
Younger men (<35), sexually activeOlder men (>35), low sexual risk
Likely causeSexually transmitted: C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeaeEnteric: E. coli (UTI/gram-negative organisms)
ContextNew/multiple partners, urethral dischargeRecent instrumentation/catheter, UTI, BPH/outflow problems
Investigation focusSTI screen (NAAT)MSU for MC&S
Causative agents: when sexually acquired, C. trachomatis (commonest) then N. gonorrhoeae; when not sexually acquired, enteric organisms — chiefly E. coli; rarely M. tuberculosis. Mumps orchitis is the classic viral cause: it follows parotitis by about 4–8 days, is usually unilateral (bilateral in a minority), is managed supportively, is vaccine-preventable (MMR) and is a notifiable disease.
Clinical Features
  • Scrotal pain and swelling — usually unilateral, developing over hours to days (more gradual than torsion)
  • Erythema of the overlying scrotum; testicular pain/tenderness
  • May have urethral discharge (STI cause), dysuria/urinary symptoms (enteric cause), fever
  • Prehn’s sign — pain relieved by elevating the testis (suggests epididymo-orchitis over torsion) — unreliable, never use it to exclude torsion
  • Cremasteric reflex usually present (contrast with torsion, where it’s typically absent)
The Critical Differential — Exclude Testicular Torsion
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side torsion vs epididymo-orchitis — sudden severe pain / high-riding horizontal testis / absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration, do NOT delay for ultrasound.
Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency and the key differential. It peaks in the teens and early twenties but occurs at any age — never exclude it because a man is “too old”. Salvage rates fall sharply beyond about 6 hours, so torsion is considered first in any acute scrotum — and a longer history does not make it safe to stop considering it.
🌀 Torsion clues
  • Sudden, severe pain, often waking the patient, with nausea/vomiting — but a history of more than a few hours does NOT exclude it
  • High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
  • Absent cremasteric reflex; no urinary symptoms; younger patient
🔥 Epididymo-orchitis clues
  • More gradual onset
  • Urinary/urethral symptoms, fever
  • Cremasteric reflex present
If torsion cannot be excluded clinically → urgent surgical scrotal exploration, NOT imaging (don’t delay for an ultrasound).
Other differentials: inguinal hernia; testicular tumour (typically painless — a red flag if a mass persists).
Investigations
  • Exclude torsion first (clinical ± urgent exploration)
  • Young / STI likely: STI screen — first-catch urine + urethral swab NAAT for chlamydia + gonorrhoea; urethral Gram stain (gram-negative intracellular diplococci → gonorrhoea)
  • Older / low sexual risk: MSU for MC&S + urine dipstick (leucocytes/nitrites → enteric/UTI cause)
  • Urethral swab for CULTURE if gonorrhoea is suspected or diplococci are seen — taken before antibiotics, because culture is the only way to get antimicrobial susceptibilities, and ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhoea is emerging
  • Scrotal ultrasound (Doppler) — assesses blood flow + supports the diagnosis, but must not delay exploration if torsion is suspected. Crucially, normal or preserved Doppler flow does NOT exclude torsion — flow can be preserved in partial or intermittent torsion, and a negative scan must never overturn a clinical suspicion that warrants exploration
Management (BASHH)

Treat empirically based on the likely cause (start before culture results):

① STI likely (young, sexually active)
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 10–14 days
  • Dose check: ceftriaxone 1 g IM — the older 500 mg dose is out of date (BASHH)
② Enteric/non-STI likely (older, low risk)
  • Ofloxacin 200 mg PO BD for 14 days, or levofloxacin 500 mg PO OD for 10 days — quinolones penetrate the testis well and cover enteric organisms
  • Fluoroquinolones may only be prescribed when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA) — counsel about tendinitis and tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm and dissection, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects, and tell the patient to stop the drug and seek advice at the first sign of tendon pain
③ Mixed STI + enteric risk (e.g. insertive anal sex): ceftriaxone 1 g IM + ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days.
General: analgesia (NSAIDs), scrotal support/elevation, rest, fluids. If STI cause: no sex until treatment complete, refer to GUM for full screen + partner notification. If not settling, re-image (?abscess, ?tumour).
Admit if: torsion or another surgical emergency has not been confidently excluded; systemic sepsis or a high fever; a suspected abscess; failure of oral therapy or inability to take it; or Fournier’s gangrene is suspected — pain out of proportion to the findings, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus or necrotic skin over the scrotum and perineum, typically in a man with diabetes or immunosuppression. That is a life-threatening necrotising fasciitis needing immediate surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Follow-up: review at 3 days if symptoms are not improving — reconsider the diagnosis and the organism. Review again at 2 weeks to confirm resolution, check adherence and complete partner notification. If gonorrhoea is confirmed, arrange a test of cure.
Complications
  • Abscess formation, testicular infarction/atrophy, hydrocele/pyocele
  • Reduced fertility (especially bilateral)
  • Chronic epididymitis / chronic scrotal pain
Exam Pearls
What it is
Infective inflammation of the epididymis ± testis; common cause of acute scrotal pain.
Must-not-miss
ALWAYS exclude testicular torsion first (surgical emergency, salvage falls off beyond ~6 h, and it happens at any age) — sudden severe pain, high-riding/horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration, don’t wait for imaging. A normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion.
Aetiology
Sexually active → chlamydia (commonest) then gonorrhoea; catheter/instrumentation/outflow problems or no sexual risk → E. coli (enteric). Age guides, risk decides.
Investigate
Young → STI screen (urine/urethral NAAT); older → MSU MC&S.
STI treatment
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 10–14 days (1 g, not the old 500 mg).
Enteric treatment
Ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days, or levofloxacin 500 mg OD for 10 days — fluoroquinolones only when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA).
STI cause
GUM referral + partner notification + no sex until treated.
Red flags
Painless mass = think tumour; Fournier’s gangrene (crepitus, necrotic skin, pain out of proportion) = immediate surgery; mumps = a non-STI orchitis cause.
Complications
Abscess, infarction/atrophy, infertility, chronic pain.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea:
What & Why

Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — the second commonest bacterial STI (after chlamydia). It causes symptomatic infection more often than chlamydia (so it presents), untreated infection causes the same serious complications (PID, infertility, ectopic) plus disseminated infection, and — above all — it’s the poster child for antimicrobial resistance: gonococci have defeated penicillins, tetracyclines + quinolones, and ceftriaxone is now the last reliable first-line agent, with resistant strains already emerging.

The organism: a gram-negative diplococcus (“coffee-bean pairs”, seen intracellularly within neutrophils). It infects mucous membranes lined by COLUMNAR epithelium — endocervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva, pharynx — not squamous vaginal epithelium (a high-yield tropism point).
Clinical Features
Symptoms are commoner than in chlamydia — but that is mainly urethral infection in men (around 90% symptomatic). About half of women with urogenital infection, and most pharyngeal and rectal infections, are asymptomatic — so asymptomatic contacts and extragenital sites still need testing.
  • Odourless purulent discharge — often green or yellow (urethral in men; endocervical/vaginal in women)
  • Dysuria
  • Pelvic pain (women) / testicular pain or swelling (men — epididymo-orchitis)
  • Rectal infection — often asymptomatic; may cause anal discomfort/discharge
  • Prostatitis — perineal pain, urinary symptoms, tender prostate
  • Conjunctivitis — erythema, purulent discharge (adult autoinoculation, or neonatal)
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Urethral Gram-stain microscopy — Gram-negative intracellular diplococci within a neutrophil, giving a rapid presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men.
  • NAAT — the primary diagnostic test: endocervical / vulvovaginal / urethral swab (or first-catch urine); rectal + pharyngeal swabs — routine in men who have sex with men and in sex workers, and pharyngeal sampling for everyone diagnosed with urogenital gonorrhoea and for every contact, whatever their gender or reported sexual history, because pharyngeal infection is usually silent and is the site most likely to fail treatment
  • ALSO take a charcoal swab for culture & sensitivities (MC&S) BEFORE treatment — essential because of high + rising resistance (NAAT confirms the organism but only culture gives sensitivities). This is what distinguishes gonorrhoea from chlamydia management
  • Urethral Gram stain — gram-negative intracellular diplococci gives a rapid presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men
Management (BASHH)
📷 Image placeholder — Treatment algorithm — ceftriaxone 1 g IM single-dose monotherapy for everyone (azithromycin dropped); ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO only when ceftriaxone cannot be used and culture confirms a sensitive isolate.

The regimen depends on whether antibiotic sensitivities are known:

① Sensitivity UNKNOWN (empirical — usual)
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose — MONOTHERAPY
  • Why monotherapy? the older regimen added azithromycin 1 g — azithromycin is now dropped (rising resistance). The 1 g ceftriaxone dose covers reduced-susceptibility strains, and dropping azithromycin reduces resistance pressure
  • If IM injection is refused or contraindicated: alternatives exist but are less reliable, especially at the pharynx — an oral cefixime-based regimen with azithromycin, or intramuscular gentamicin with azithromycin. Use these on specialist advice, and a test of cure is mandatory because they are not first-line
② Susceptibility KNOWN (culture result back)
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IM stays first line even when the isolate is ciprofloxacin-sensitive
  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose is no longer a routine alternative — reserve it for people who cannot have ceftriaxone (e.g. severe cephalosporin allergy), and only when culture confirms a sensitive isolate. Quinolones should be used only when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA)
Test of cure (TOC) — don’t skip it. It is recommended for: pharyngeal infection; persistent symptoms or signs; susceptibility unknown (no culture result — which covers most people diagnosed on NAAT alone); anyone treated with something other than ceftriaxone; and pregnancy. Routine TOC is only unnecessary for uncomplicated anogenital infection treated with ceftriaxone 1 g where culture has confirmed a ceftriaxone-susceptible isolate. Timing: NAAT at least 2 weeks after treatment (earlier and it picks up dead organisms → false positive); culture at least 72 hours after finishing treatment if symptoms or signs persist.
General advice: no sex until 7 days after both the patient and partner(s) have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Refer to GUM; partner notification / contact tracing. Look-back: for men with symptomatic urethral infection, partners from the 2 weeks before symptom onset (or the last partner if longer ago); for everyone else — asymptomatic infection, women, and extragenital sites — the preceding 3 months. Test for other STIs (chlamydia co-infection is common — but treat gonorrhoea specifically). Pregnancy: ceftriaxone 1 g IM is unchanged and safe, but doxycycline is contraindicated, so treat coexisting chlamydia with azithromycin — and a test of cure is recommended. Untreated maternal infection is what causes ophthalmia neonatorum.
Key Complications
👶 Neonatal / emergency
  • Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) — from the mother at birth; a medical emergency → can cause corneal perforation + blindness, associated with sepsis. It presents in the first few days of life (chlamydial conjunctivitis presents later, around 5–14 days). Action: same-day ophthalmology and paediatric review, eye swabs for NAAT and culture, frequent saline irrigation, and a systemic third-generation cephalosporin — topical treatment alone is not enough. Test and treat the mother and her partner(s)
🩸 Disseminated (DGI)
  • Haematogenous spread — the classic triad: dermatitis (pustular/haemorrhagic skin lesions), migratory polyarthritis/arthralgia, tenosynovitis
  • (± later purulent septic arthritis, rarely endocarditis/meningitis)
  • Not a single-dose illness: discuss with sexual health — ceftriaxone given daily for at least a week, guided by blood, joint and mucosal cultures. Sample all mucosal sites even if the genital tract is asymptomatic, as that is usually where the organism is found
  • Local: PID → infertility, ectopic (women); epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis (men); urethral strictures
  • Increased HIV transmission
Exam Pearls
Organism / tropism
N. gonorrhoeae = gram-negative diplococcus; infects COLUMNAR epithelium (endocervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva, pharynx) — not squamous vagina.
vs chlamydia
More often symptomatic — but mainly urethral infection in men; about half of women, and most pharyngeal/rectal infections, are asymptomatic. Purulent green/yellow discharge + dysuria.
Diagnose
NAAT + ALWAYS a charcoal swab for culture & sensitivities (because of resistance).
1st-line
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose — MONOTHERAPY (azithromycin now dropped).
Ciprofloxacin
Not routine. Only when ceftriaxone cannot be used AND culture confirms a sensitive isolate (MHRA quinolone caution).
TOC
Needed for pharyngeal infection, persisting symptoms, unknown susceptibility, non-ceftriaxone treatment and pregnancy — so in practice most patients. NAAT ≥2 weeks; culture ≥72 h if still symptomatic.
Advice
GUM referral; partner notification (2 weeks for symptomatic urethral infection in men, otherwise 3 months); no sex until 7 days after the patient and partners finish treatment.
Complications
Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum — emergency, blindness), DGI (dermatitis + migratory polyarthritis + tenosynovitis), PID/infertility.
AMR
Ceftriaxone is the last reliable first-line agent; resistant strains emerging.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical staging, AR:
What & Why

HIV is a retrovirus that infects and destroys CD4 T-helper cells, progressively crippling cell-mediated immunity until the patient becomes vulnerable to opportunistic infections and malignancies — the point at which it becomes AIDS. It’s a chronic, treatable, lifelong condition where modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) gives near-normal life expectancy and renders the person sexually non-infectious (U=U); and where prevention (PrEP, PEP) and preventing vertical transmission are highly examinable.

The organism: HIV is an RNA retrovirus — HIV-1 (commonest worldwide) and HIV-2 (less common, West Africa). It enters + destroys CD4 T-helper cells; AIDS occurs when depletion leaves the patient immunocompromised.
Transmission
  • Unprotected anal, vaginal, or oral sex (anal receptive = highest risk)
  • Vertical transmission (in utero, at delivery, breastfeeding)
  • Infected blood/body fluids — needlestick, sharing needles, mucous-membrane/open-wound exposure
U=U (“Undetectable = Untransmittable”): a person on effective ART with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV sexually — a foundational modern principle that transforms counselling and reduces stigma. It requires continued adherence and sustained suppression (usually for at least 6 months), and it refers to sexual transmission: a small residual risk remains with breastfeeding.
Natural History & Clinical Stages

Primary HIV / seroconversion2–4 weeks post-infection: glandular-fever-like illness (fever, malaise, maculopapular rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers). Often missed; very infectious

2

↓
3
