AIDS-Defining Illnesses
📷 Image placeholder — CD4 threshold ladder — opportunistic infections by count (PCP <200, CMV/MAC <50, TB at any CD4).
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) — dry cough, exertional desaturation (CD4 <200)
  • Kaposi’s sarcoma — caused by HHV-8; purple papules/plaques on skin/mucosa (GI/respiratory); radiotherapy/resection ± systemic therapy
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) — retinitis, colitis (CD4 <50)
  • Oesophageal/bronchial candidiasis
  • Lymphomas (including CNS lymphoma — EBV)
  • Tuberculosis (any CD4 — commonest globally)
  • Also: cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML
Diagnosis & Monitoring
Diagnosis: 4th-generation lab test (HIV antibody + p24 antigen) — the UK standard screening test. It detects most infections from about 4 weeks, but the window period is 45 days (about 6 weeks): a negative test taken sooner than 45 days after the last exposure does not exclude HIV and must be repeated at 45 days. A reactive screening test is not a diagnosis — it needs confirming on a second laboratory assay. Point-of-care and self-tests are available but have a longer window, and any reactive result needs laboratory confirmation.
Who to test: anyone who asks; anyone with a possible seroconversion illness or an HIV indicator condition (unexplained weight loss, recurrent shingles, oral candidiasis, unexplained lymphadenopathy, TB, PCP, Kaposi’s sarcoma); everyone attending a sexual health service and everyone diagnosed with another STI; and universal opt-out screening — every pregnant person at booking, and, in areas of high (≥2 per 1,000) or extremely high (≥5 per 1,000) diagnosed prevalence, emergency department attendees having bloods, new GP registrations and general medical admissions. HIV testing does not need specialist counselling — any clinician can take consent (NICE, UKHSA, BHIVA).
🔢 CD4 count (normal 500–1200 cells/mm³)
  • <200 = high risk of opportunistic infections / AIDS
🧬 HIV viral load (RNA copies/mL)
  • Marker of viral activity; thousands+ if untreated
  • Goal = undetectable (<50 copies/mL) on ART
Management — Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) (BHIVA)
ART is offered to EVERYONE with HIV, regardless of CD4 count (start as soon as possible after diagnosis).
  • Drug classes: NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors (INSTI), entry inhibitors
  • Standard first-line: 2 NRTIs + a third agent (now usually an integrase inhibitor) — e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + dolutegravir
  • Aim: sustained undetectable viral load → immune recovery + U=U
  • Long-acting injectable ART given every 2 months is now an option for some people who are already virologically suppressed and prefer not to take daily tablets
Additional care: CD4 <200 → prophylactic co-trimoxazole against PCP (also if there is oral candidiasis or a previous AIDS-defining illness); it can be stopped once ART has held the CD4 above 200 for about 3 months. Partner notification — offer testing to current and recent partners, and to any children of a newly diagnosed woman. Annual cervical smears (↑ HPV/cervical cancer risk). Vaccinations (avoid live vaccines if severely immunosuppressed), CVD risk management, bone/renal monitoring, mental health support.
Preventing Vertical Transmission
  • Mode of delivery by maternal viral load at 36 weeks: <50 copies/mL → planned vaginal delivery; 50–399 → planned pre-labour caesarean is recommended, weighing the actual value, its trajectory, time on ART and adherence; 400 or more → pre-labour caesarean
  • Unknown/>1000 copies/mL → IV zidovudine during labour
  • Neonatal prophylaxis: start as soon as possible after birth. Low-risk (mother on ART with viral load <50) → zidovudine alone for 2–4 weeks; high-risk → combination prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine) for 4 weeks. The infant is then tested by HIV PCR at set intervals, because maternal antibody persists and antibody testing is uninterpretable
  • Infant feeding: formula feeding is recommended, because it carries no risk of postnatal transmission. If the mother is fully suppressed (viral load <50) and adherent and chooses to breastfeed, she should be supported, not refused — but counselled that the risk is low, not zero, that feeding should be exclusive (mixed feeding is discouraged), and with monthly maternal viral load and infant testing during breastfeeding and for 2 months after stopping (BHIVA)
Prevention — PrEP & PEP
🛡️ PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis)
  • ART taken by HIV-NEGATIVE people at ongoing risk to prevent acquisition
  • Tenofovir disoproxil + emtricitabine — daily, or event-based (“2-1-1”) dosing, which is only suitable for anal sex (not for vaginal sex)
  • Confirm the person is HIV-negative before starting — starting two-drug PrEP in undiagnosed HIV risks drug resistance. Then HIV testing and an STI screen roughly every 3 months, plus renal function at baseline and periodically, and hepatitis B status
  • Highly effective against HIV with good adherence, but gives no protection against other STIs or pregnancy — condoms and regular STI screening still matter
💊 PEP (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis)
  • ART started AFTER a potential exposure to prevent seroconversion
  • Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of the exposure — ideally within 24 hours; PEP is not recommended beyond 72 hours
  • Regimen: tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir (or dolutegravir) for 28 days
  • HIV test at baseline, then a repeat 4th-generation test 45 days after finishing the course — for sexual exposures usually done at 12 weeks after the exposure, alongside repeat syphilis testing. Covers sexual (PEPSE) and occupational (needlestick) exposure; screen for other STIs and hepatitis B, and consider PrEP afterwards if the risk is ongoing
Exam Pearls
What it is
RNA retrovirus destroying CD4 T-helper cells; HIV-1 (common) / HIV-2. AIDS = immunocompromise from CD4 depletion.
Seroconversion
Glandular-fever-like (fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy) 2–4 weeks post-infection.
Diagnose / monitor
4th-gen antibody/p24 antigen test; window period 45 days — an earlier negative does not exclude HIV. CD4 (<200 = AIDS risk) + viral load (goal undetectable). Opt-out testing: all pregnant people at booking, and ED/GP/medical admissions in high-prevalence areas.
U=U
Undetectable viral load = cannot transmit sexually.
ART
For everyone: 2 NRTIs + an integrase inhibitor (e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + dolutegravir).
Prophylaxis
CD4 <200 → co-trimoxazole PCP prophylaxis. Annual cervical smears.
AIDS illnesses
PCP, Kaposi’s (HHV-8), CMV, oesophageal candida, TB, lymphoma, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus.
Vertical transmission
By viral load at 36 weeks: <50 → vaginal; 50 or more → pre-labour CS; unknown or >1000 → IV zidovudine in labour. Neonatal prophylaxis from birth; formula feeding recommended.
PrEP / PEP
PrEP (tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine, daily or event-based for anal sex) = HIV-negative, prevent acquisition; exclude HIV first; no cover against other STIs. PEP (tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir, 28 days) = after exposure, start within 72 h.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital Warts:
What & Why

Genital warts are benign epithelial growths caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV) — the one of the commonest STIs diagnosed in UK sexual health services (chlamydia, gonorrhoea and genital herpes are diagnosed more often). They’re very common, highly transmissible, benign but distressing, and open the door to the broader HPV story — the same virus family causes cervical, anal, vulval, vaginal, penile + oropharyngeal cancers, which is why HPV vaccination and cervical screening are woven in.

The core distinction — low-risk vs high-risk HPV: HPV 6 & 11 cause warts; HPV 16 & 18 cause cancer — and the 9-valent vaccine covers both.
🟢 HPV 6 & 11 (“low-risk”)
  • Cause ~90% of genital warts
  • Do NOT cause cancer
🔴 HPV 16 & 18 (“high-risk”)
  • Cause ~70% of cervical cancer (+ other anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers)
  • Do NOT typically cause warts
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical photograph — condylomata acuminata: soft non-keratinised (podophyllotoxin) vs firm keratinised (cryotherapy) morphology guiding treatment.
  • Painless lumps on the genitals or anal area
  • Either keratinised (hard) or non-keratinised (soft) — a distinction that guides treatment
  • Areas traumatised during intercourse commonly affected (introitus, penis, perianal skin)
  • May be single or multiple; occasionally itch, bleed, or cause distress; usually a clinical diagnosis (biopsy only if atypical/pigmented/suspicious)
Management (BASHH)

Choice guided by number/type/site + patient preference:

1️⃣ First-line
  • Topical podophyllotoxin — best for multiple, non-keratinised (soft) warts; patient-applied at home
  • Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) — best for solitary, keratinised (hard) warts; clinician-applied
2️⃣ Second-line / resistant
  • Topical imiquimod (immune-response modifier) — larger/keratinised warts or if 1st-line fails; patient-applied; suitable for keratinised or non-keratinised warts, and useful if first-line fails or is not tolerated
  • Trichloroacetic acid, surgical excision/electrocautery/laser — difficult, extensive, or recurrent warts
BASHH: no single treatment is superior — choice by patient preference, wart morphology + site; patients can switch if response is limited.
Key principles
  • Recurrence is common (~30%) — warn the patient; warts can recur after apparent clearance
  • Formal contact tracing/partner notification is NOT required (unlike bacterial STIs) — but current partners should be offered assessment and a full STI screen
🤰 Pregnancy + wider care
  • Podophyllotoxin + imiquimod are contraindicated → use cryotherapy (rarely, extensive warts → neonatal laryngeal papillomatosis)
  • Offer a full STI screen; discuss psychosexual wellbeing; encourage HPV vaccination if eligible (catch-up to 25, MSM to 45, at-risk groups) + continued cervical screening
HPV Vaccination & Cervical Screening (the prevention story)
📷 Image placeholder — Current UK HPV schedule — School Year 8, both sexes, single dose; MSM eligible to age 45.
  • The current UK vaccine is 9-valent — it protects against HPV 6, 11 (warts) + 16, 18 (cancer) plus five more high-risk types
  • UK programme: offered to all children in school Year 8 (age 12–13), both boys and girls — now a single dose. anyone who misses the school offer can catch up until their 25th birthday. Also offered to MSM up to and including age 45 via sexual health/HIV services (single dose if under 25, 2 doses if 25 or over), with a 3-dose schedule for those who are immunosuppressed or living with HIV (UKHSA)
  • UK cervical screening: women and people with a cervix aged 25–64 — the sample is tested for high-risk HPV first, with cytology only as a triage test on HPV-positive samples
  • HPV-negative → routine recall in 5 years (in England the 25–49 interval has moved from 3- to 5-yearly, matching 50–64). HPV-positive with normal cytology → repeat in 12 months. HPV-positive with abnormal cytology → colposcopy
  • Vaccination does not replace screening, and genital warts are not an indication to change screening — types 6 and 11 are not oncogenic (UK NSC)
  • Given before sexual debut for maximum benefit — has dramatically reduced both genital warts and pre-cancerous cervical lesions where uptake is high
Exam Pearls
What it is
Genital warts = HPV, usually types 6 & 11 (low-risk, ~90% of warts, benign).
High-risk HPV
16 & 18 → ~70% of cervical cancer (different types from warts).
Features
Painless keratinised (hard) or non-keratinised (soft) anogenital lumps.
1st-line
Podophyllotoxin (multiple soft warts) or cryotherapy (solitary hard warts). 2nd-line: imiquimod (keratinised or soft warts).
Key points
Recurrence ~30% is common. Contact tracing NOT required (contrast with bacterial STIs).
Pregnancy
Avoid podophyllotoxin/imiquimod → cryotherapy.
Vaccine
The 9-valent vaccine (Year 8, both sexes, single dose) covers 6/11 + 16/18 → prevents warts AND cancer.
Screening
HPV-primary testing with cytology triage, ages 25–64, 5-yearly if HPV-negative. Vaccination does not replace it; warts do not change it.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital):
What & Why

Genital herpes is a chronic, recurrent, sexually transmitted viral infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). It’s extremely common, incurable (lifelong latency with recurrences), causes painful genital ulceration, and — most importantly for exams — carries a serious risk of neonatal herpes if a woman acquires it near delivery, which drives specific pregnancy management.

The mechanism: after initial infection, the virus becomes latent in the sensory nerve ganglia — the trigeminal ganglion for cold sores, the sacral ganglia for genital herpes — and reactivates to cause recurrent episodes.
HSV-1
  • Classically cold sores (oral), often acquired in childhood, dormant in the trigeminal ganglion
  • Genital HSV-1, acquired through oro-genital sex, is now the commonest cause of first-episode genital herpes in the UK, particularly in young adults — but it recurs less often than HSV-2
HSV-2
  • Typically causes genital herpes; mostly an STI
  • Tends to recur more often than genital HSV-1
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical photo — grouped vesicles on an erythematous base evolving to shallow painful ulcers/crusting (the hallmark morphology).
  • May be asymptomatic, or symptoms appear months/years later on reactivation; when symptomatic, features usually appear within ~2 weeks of exposure
  • Painful genital ulceration or vesicular (blistering) lesions — the hallmark (vesicles → painful ulcers → crusting)
  • PRIMARY (first) infection is more severe than recurrences — systemic symptoms (headache, fever, malaise), extensive painful lesions, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy
  • Dysuria (from lesions); sometimes urinary retention (severe primary) or aseptic meningitis (rare)
  • Recurrent episodes — shorter, milder, often preceded by a prodrome (tingling/burning), and less frequent over time
Investigations
  • NAAT (HSV PCR) of a swab from the lesion base — the test of choice (de-roof a vesicle and swab the base; it also types HSV-1 vs HSV-2)
  • HSV serology (type-specific antibodies) — useful in recurrent ulceration of unknown cause, or to establish whether a pregnancy episode is primary vs recurrent
Management (BASHH)
No cure — treatment shortens episodes + reduces severity/transmission. Advise saline bathing, simple analgesia, topical lidocaine ointment, fluids, and abstaining from sex while lesions are present. For painful urination, advise passing urine while sitting in a bath or with water poured over the area. Urinary retention is the commonest reason for hospital admission in a first episode — if conservative measures fail, catheterisation is needed (a suprapubic catheter may give better symptom control than a urethral one).
🔴 First (primary) episode
  • Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days (start within 5 days of onset or while new lesions forming)
  • Valaciclovir 500 mg BD for 5 days is an alternative. Cold sores → topical aciclovir
🔁 Recurrent episodes
  • Often mild + self-limiting → supportive care may suffice
  • Episodic antiviral started at the prodrome or within 24–48 h — e.g. aciclovir 800 mg three times daily for 2 days — for troublesome recurrences
  • Suppressive therapy for frequent recurrences (≥6/year): aciclovir 400 mg BD (or valaciclovir 500 mg OD)
SH measures: GUM referral, full STI screen, discuss transmission (shedding occurs even when asymptomatic → condoms reduce but don’t eliminate risk), psychological support. Formal partner notification is not indicated and genital herpes is not notifiable (as with warts), but the current partner should be offered assessment and advice, and the patient supported in disclosing to partners.
Herpes in Pregnancy & Neonatal HSV (BASHH/RCOG)
📷 Image placeholder — Decision flowchart — primary vs recurrent × gestation (>28 wk / <28 wk / recurrent) → antivirals + mode of delivery (elective CS vs vaginal if no lesions at term).
The danger: neonatal HSV is contracted mainly from active genital lesions/viral shedding during vaginal delivery → devastating disseminated/CNS disease. Risk is highest when the mother acquires a FIRST episode in the third trimester (no time to develop/transfer protective antibodies). Neonatal herpes presents in the first 4 weeks (typically around day 5–14) in three patterns: localised skin, eye and mouth disease; CNS disease (seizures, lethargy, poor feeding); and disseminated disease (sepsis-like illness, jaundice, respiratory distress, coagulopathy). Most infants with disseminated disease are afebrile and have no skin lesions, so it mimics bacterial sepsis, and mortality is high. Treat with intravenous aciclovir — started empirically in any neonate with sepsis, seizures or unexplained deterioration in whom HSV is possible, without waiting for confirmation.
🤰 Primary infection in pregnancy
  • First episode >28 weeks (3rd trimester): caesarean section recommended, particularly if within 6 weeks of delivery — transmission risk is very high (around 40%) because there is no time to make and transfer protective antibodies. Send type-specific serology: if she is seronegative for the HSV type found on PCR this is a true primary infection and caesarean is recommended; if antibodies to that type are already present the episode is a recurrence and caesarean is not indicated. Treat with oral aciclovir, then suppressive aciclovir 400 mg TDS until delivery
  • First episode <28 weeks: treat the episode; suppressive aciclovir 400 mg TDS from 36 weeks; vaginal delivery if no lesions at term
🔁 Recurrent genital herpes in pregnancy
  • Much lower neonatal risk (maternal antibodies protect the baby)
  • Suppressive aciclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks is offered to reduce the chance of lesions at term (a higher dose than the 400 mg twice daily used outside pregnancy); vaginal delivery is appropriate, including when lesions are present at labour
  • Active lesions at the onset of labour are NOT in themselves an indication for caesarean in recurrent disease — the risk of neonatal herpes is low (0–3%). Plan vaginal delivery unless there is another obstetric indication, avoid fetal scalp electrodes and fetal blood sampling, and inform the neonatal team
Breastfeeding: aciclovir/valaciclovir are safe (minimal transfer). Avoid direct lesion contact with the baby; cold-sore precautions (no kissing the neonate).
Exam Pearls
Mechanism
HSV-1 or HSV-2; latent in SACRAL ganglia (genital) / trigeminal (oral), reactivates.
Strains
HSV-1 = usually oral/cold sores (genital via oro-genital sex); HSV-2 = usually genital, recurs more.
Features
Painful vesicles → ulcers; PRIMARY episode severe (fever, malaise, tender inguinal nodes); recurrences milder.
Diagnose
HSV PCR on a swab from the base of a de-roofed vesicle or ulcer (also types HSV-1 vs HSV-2). Type-specific serology has a limited role.
Treatment
1st episode: oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS × 5 days. Frequent recurrences (≥6/yr): suppressive aciclovir 400 mg BD.
Key points
No cure; shedding occurs when asymptomatic; contact tracing not required.
Pregnancy — primary
PRIMARY infection >28 weeks → elective caesarean + aciclovir + suppression to delivery.
Pregnancy — other
Primary <28 weeks or recurrent disease → suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks, vaginal delivery if no lesions at term.
Neonatal
Neonatal HSV risk highest with maternal primary infection near term.
SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH framing):
What & Why — the GUM-Clinic Angle
📷 Image placeholder — Ascending infection pathway — endocervix → endometritis → salpingitis → oophoritis → pelvic peritonitis, showing how a silent STI becomes tubal damage.

In sexual health, PID matters as the most important preventable complication of untreated bacterial STIs — where an ascending chlamydia or gonorrhoea infection stops being a local, silent problem and starts causing tubal damage, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. The GUM priority: very low threshold to treat empirically, identify + treat the causative STI, and notify + treat partners — PID is a sentinel event flagging an STI in the patient and their sexual network.

The core route: infection ascends from the endocervix → endometritis → salpingitis → oophoritis → pelvic peritonitis. The causative STIs are the same ones you screen for — which is why PID + STI screening are inseparable in GUM. (See the Obs & Gynae “Pelvic & Vaginal Infections” note for the full clinical work-up.)
The Decisive Fork (SH version) — Which STI Is Driving It?
OrganismGUM significance
Chlamydia trachomatisCommonest cause — often silent, so PID may be the first sign of infection
Neisseria gonorrhoeaeCauses more severe PID; drives the ceftriaxone-based regimen
Mycoplasma genitaliumIncreasingly recognised; may need specific (moxifloxacin) cover
Anaerobes / endogenous floraWhy metronidazole is included
GUM framing: gonorrhoea or chlamydia are identified on testing in up to a quarter of UK PID cases — but a negative STI test does NOT exclude PID (many cases are polymicrobial or test-negative), so you treat on clinical suspicion regardless.
Clinical Features
  • Lower abdominal pain (usually bilateral), deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, abnormal bleeding (IMB/PCB), fever, dysuria
  • On examination: cervical motion tenderness (“cervical excitation”) — the classic sign — plus adnexal/pelvic tenderness and cervicitis
Exclude first — the low threshold to treat does not mean skipping the differential: ectopic pregnancy (β-hCG in every case — PID is the commonest misdiagnosis in a missed ectopic), appendicitis (usually unilateral right iliac fossa pain, anorexia), ovarian cyst rupture or torsion, UTI, endometriosis and functional pain. Peritonism, unilateral pain or shock means think surgical, not “start doxycycline and review”.
Investigations — the STI-Screen-Driven Workup
  • Pregnancy test (β-hCG) — always: to exclude ectopic pregnancy, and because a positive test changes management (see below)
  • NAAT (endocervical/vulvovaginal swab) for chlamydia AND gonorrhoea — the central GUM test; also consider Mycoplasma genitalium
  • High vaginal swab for BV, candida, trichomonas
  • Microscopy (immediate-access wet mount/Gram stain) — absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely (a useful rule-out), but it does not override a strong clinical picture, it is unavailable in most non-GUM settings, and it says nothing about the surgical differentials; CRP/ESR often raised
  • Full STI screen including HIV + syphilis serology — because PID signals sexual-risk exposure
Key principle: PID is a clinical diagnosis — a negative swab doesn’t exclude it → start empirical treatment on suspicion rather than wait for results.
Management — with the GUM/Partner Dimension (BASHH)
Have a LOW threshold for empirical treatment — the diagnosis is uncertain and the complications of delay (infertility, ectopic, chronic pain) are serious.
✅ First-line (outpatient, mild–moderate)
  • IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose
  • + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days
  • + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days
Second-line
  • Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days
  • Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg OD 14 days — the option of choice if Mycoplasma genitalium is identified or suspected
  • Per MHRA fluoroquinolone safety advice, quinolones are otherwise second-line; avoid if gonococcal PID is likely (resistance)
If the pregnancy test is positive: exclude ectopic pregnancy first. PID in pregnancy is rare but serious — admit, discuss with obstetrics and give parenteral antibiotics. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, as are the quinolones (ofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — never give the standard outpatient regimen to a pregnant woman.
Admit for IV antibiotics if: a surgical emergency cannot be excluded (ectopic, appendicitis); severe illness or sepsis (high fever, peritonism, vomiting); tubo-ovarian abscess; pregnancy; or failure of, or inability to tolerate, oral therapy. IV therapy continues until about 24 h after clinical improvement, then switches to oral to complete 14 days in total.
The defining GUM step — partners: refer to GUM and notify/contact-trace — current + recent partners (look back ~6 months) should be assessed, tested, and treated empirically (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) to prevent “ping-pong” re-infection. No sex until the patient AND partner(s) have completed treatment.
In mild–moderate PID an intrauterine device can usually be left in situ if she is improving by 48–72 hours; if she is not improving, or the PID is severe, the device should usually be removed — and if it is removed, consider emergency contraception where there has been unprotected sex in the preceding 7 days. Test for other STIs (HIV, syphilis). Review at 48–72 hours; if not improving, reconsider the diagnosis and consider admission (tubo-ovarian abscess). Review again after the course to confirm resolution, that the 14 days were completed and that partners were treated. Safety-net: worsening pain, fever or rigors, vomiting, heavy bleeding or feeling faint → seek urgent review.
Complications (the STI-Sequelae Emphasis)
📷 Image placeholder — Laparoscopic 'violin-string' perihepatic adhesions of Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (RUQ pain in PID).
  • Tubal factor infertility — risk rises with each PID episode (a key reason to treat STIs early)
  • Ectopic pregnancy (tubal scarring)
  • Chronic pelvic pain
  • Tubo-ovarian abscess (may need drainage/admission)
  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome — perihepatitis (RUQ pain + “violin-string” adhesions) from ascending chlamydial/gonococcal infection
Exam Pearls (SH-oriented)
What it is
Ascending endocervical infection; commonest STI cause = Chlamydia (gonorrhoea = more severe).
Classic sign
Cervical motion tenderness (excitation).
Always
β-hCG (exclude ectopic) + NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea + full STI screen. Absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely.
Threshold
LOW threshold to treat empirically — don’t wait for swabs.
1st-line (outpatient)
IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 100 mg BD 14d + metronidazole 400 mg BD 14d (quinolones now 2nd-line, MHRA; moxifloxacin if M. genitalium).
Admit if
Surgical emergency not excluded, sepsis/severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, PREGNANCY (doxycycline and quinolones contraindicated), or failing/not tolerating oral therapy.
Defining GUM step
GUM referral + partner notification/treatment + no sex until both treated.
Complications
Infertility, ectopic, chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies:
What & Why

Scabies is an intensely itchy skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, which burrows into the stratum corneum to lay eggs. It’s very common (UK care-home + household outbreaks), a key cause of generalised itch, can be sexually transmitted (hence its place in GUM as well as dermatology), and treatment failure is almost always a technique/contact problem rather than drug failure.

The core mechanism: the female mite burrows + lays eggs. The itch is a delayed type IV (T-cell) hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs + faeces — NOT the mite directly. This explains: (1) first infestation → symptoms at 4–6 weeks (time to sensitise); (2) re-infestation → itch within 1–3 days; (3) itch persists for weeks AFTER successful treatment — usually settling over 2–6 weeks but occasionally longer (the immune reaction outlasts the dead mites) — not treatment failure.
Transmission
  • Prolonged skin-to-skin contact (the main route) — household, sexual partners, care settings
  • Sexual transmission — why it appears in GUM (genital lesions in adults)
  • Fomites (bedding/clothing) — a minor route in classic scabies (but major in crusted)
  • NOT related to poor hygiene — affects all social classes (a common misconception)
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Pathognomonic burrows — thin, wavy greyish lines in the finger web spaces and flexor wrists, with excoriated papules.
  • Intense itch, characteristically WORSE AT NIGHT — the hallmark
  • Burrows — thin, greyish, wavy lines (mm–1 cm), the pathognomonic sign, best in finger web spaces, wrists (flexor), sides of fingers
  • Erythematous papules, excoriations, secondary eczematisation from scratching
  • Distribution: finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, waist/belt line, buttocks; in adults the genitals (penis/scrotum — often nodular; breasts/nipples in women)
  • In children under 2, the elderly and the immunosuppressed: can involve the face, scalp and neck — characteristically spared in adults — as well as prominent palm and sole involvement
  • Household clustering — multiple itchy family members is a strong clue
Diagnosis
  • Largely CLINICAL — itch + burrows + typical distribution + affected contacts
  • Dermoscopy — the “delta-wing jet” sign (the mite at the end of a burrow)
  • Skin scraping microscopy — mites, eggs, or faecal pellets confirm it (low sensitivity; a negative doesn’t exclude)
The Decisive Fork — Classic vs Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side — sparse burrows of classic scabies vs thick hyperkeratotic warty crusts of crusted (Norwegian) scabies (very high mite burden, often minimal itch).
Classic scabiesCrusted (Norwegian) scabies
Mite burdenA few (~10–15 mites)Thousands–millions
WhoAnyoneImmunocompromised, elderly, frail (HIV, steroids, learning disability)
AppearanceBurrows, papules, itchThick, hyperkeratotic, warty crusts; itch may be mild/absent
TransmissibilityModerateExtremely high (outbreaks)
TreatmentTopical permethrin ×2Topical scabicide + oral ivermectin (repeated) + isolation
Crusted scabies is a public-health emergency in institutions — it looks like psoriasis/eczema but is teeming with mites → isolate, involve dermatology/specialist services urgently, alert infection prevention and control and the local health protection team, treat with a topical scabicide PLUS repeated oral ivermectin, and screen and treat all contacts.
Management (NICE)
First-line: permethrin 5% cream. Success hinges on technique:
  • Apply to the WHOLE body from the neck down (adults) — including finger/toe webs, under the nails, genitals, buttocks, soles. In children under 2, the elderly and the immunocompromised, also treat the head, face, scalp and neck (avoiding the eyes)
  • Apply to cool, dry skin — NOT straight after a hot bath (a hot bath increases absorption and washes the drug away from where it is needed)
  • Prescribe enough: an average adult needs about 30 g (one tube) per application, so at least two tubes for the full course — under-prescribing means incomplete application
  • Leave on 8–12 hours (e.g. overnight), then wash off; reapply to the hands if washed during the window
  • REPEAT the whole application after 7 days — the second dose kills newly hatched mites (eggs survive the first). Omitting the second dose is the commonest cause of “treatment failure”
💊 Second-line / alternatives
  • Malathion 0.5% AQUEOUS liquid — if permethrin is unsuitable. Leave on 24 hours (not 8–12 h like permethrin) and repeat after 7 days. Use the aqueous preparation, not an alcoholic lotion (irritant on excoriated skin)
  • Oral ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg with food, repeated after 7 days — licensed in the UK for scabies and, in adult sexual health services, an accepted alternative to permethrin for uncomplicated scabies (BASHH). Also used for crusted scabies (always WITH a topical agent), treatment failure, outbreaks, and when topical treatment is impractical. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding and under 15 kg
🚨 Critical universal steps
  • Treat ALL household members, sexual partners and close skin contacts from the preceding 8 weeks at the SAME TIME — even if asymptomatic (pre-symptomatic window) — the key step to prevent “ping-pong” re-infestation
  • No sex or other close skin contact until the patient AND all contacts have completed treatment
  • Decontaminate — wash clothing/bedding/towels at ≥50–60°C and/or seal in a bag for 72 h (mites die off-host in ~3 days)
Post-scabetic itch: emollients, crotamiton 10% cream or a mild topical corticosteroid (once the mites are eradicated), + a sedating antihistamine at night to aid sleep and reduce scratching (NICE) — and reassure it doesn’t mean failure. But it IS failure or re-infestation if new burrows or visible mites appear more than 7 days after completing treatment, or the itch is still worsening beyond 2–4 weeks after the last application → re-treat the index case AND the contacts. Sexual contacts → consider GUM referral + full STI screen (scabies as an STI marker).
Complications
  • Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginisation — Staph/Strep) from scratching → and post-streptococcal complications (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis / APSGN) in endemic settings
  • Crusted scabies → widespread outbreaks, secondary sepsis in the frail
  • Nodular scabies — persistent itchy nodules (genitals/groin) that can outlast treatment
Exam Pearls
What it is
Sarcoptes scabiei mite burrowing into skin; itch is a type IV hypersensitivity to the mite.
Presentation
Intense itch WORSE AT NIGHT + burrows in finger webs/wrists + household clustering + genital lesions.
Timing
First infestation → itch at 4–6 weeks; re-infestation → 1–3 days; itch persists 2–6 weeks AFTER cure (not failure).
1st-line
Permethrin 5% — whole body neck-down (+ head/face/scalp in under-2s, elderly, immunosuppressed), cool dry skin, 8–12 h, REPEAT at 7 days. Malathion 0.5% aqueous is left on 24 h.
Universal steps
Treat ALL close contacts from the past 8 weeks simultaneously; no sex until everyone has finished; decontaminate bedding/clothing (hot wash / bag 72 h).
Crusted (Norwegian)
Immunocompromised, thousands of mites, hyperkeratotic crusts, highly contagious → permethrin + oral ivermectin + isolate.
Post-scabetic itch
Emollient ± crotamiton/mild steroid + a SEDATING antihistamine at night. New burrows >7 days after finishing = real failure.
Complications / notes
Secondary bacterial infection (± post-strep GN), nodular scabies. NOT about hygiene; can be sexually transmitted → consider STI screen.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (NGU):
What & Why

Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra — the commonest STI presentation in men, typically causing dysuria and/or urethral discharge. It’s a syndrome, not a single organism — the first job is to split it into gonococcal (treat as gonorrhoea) vs non-gonococcal (NGU), then recognise that the leading NGU pathogens (chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium) drive both treatment and the growing problem of macrolide resistance.

Framing: presents with dysuria and/or urethral discharge — or asymptomatic. Divided into gonococcal urethritis and non-specific/non-gonococcal urethritis (NSU/NGU) — the first fork.
The Decisive Fork — Gonococcal or Non-Gonococcal?
Gonococcal urethritisNon-gonococcal (NGU/NSU)
OrganismNeisseria gonorrhoeaeChlamydia, M. genitalium, Ureaplasma, others
DischargeOften profuse, purulent, green/yellowOften scant, mucoid/clear
MicroscopyGram-negative intracellular diplococci presentPus cells (≥5 PMNs/hpf) but no diplococci
ManagementCulture for susceptibility first, then treat as gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose)Doxycycline (see below)
Causes of NGU
  • Chlamydia trachomatis — the commonest identifiable cause (~a third of NGU)
  • Mycoplasma genitalium — the second commonest; increasingly important because of macrolide resistance
  • Ureaplasma urealyticum — only inconsistently associated with NGU, and not routinely tested for; Ureaplasma parvum is not regarded as a cause
  • Others: Trichomonas vaginalis, adenovirus, HSV, and non-infective/mechanical causes (trauma, catheter). A significant proportion are idiopathic
Clinical Features
  • Dysuria and/or urethral discharge (the key symptoms) — but many cases are asymptomatic
  • Urethral discomfort/itch, meatal irritation
  • Complications of untreated NGU: epididymo-orchitis (scrotal pain — always exclude testicular torsion first in a young man), sexually acquired reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis, most often after chlamydia), and in female partners PID with tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy
  • Mycoplasma genitalium shares this profile — epididymitis, cervicitis, endometritis, PID, reactive arthritis, preterm delivery, tubal infertility (chlamydia-like)
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Urethral Gram-stain smear — ≥5 PMNs/hpf confirms urethritis; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicate gonorrhoea (absent in NGU).
  • NAAT — for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and M. genitalium: first-catch (first-void) urine in men; vulvovaginal swab in women
  • Urethral smear microscopy — confirms urethritis (≥5 polymorphs/high-power field) + looks for gram-negative intracellular diplococci (→ gonorrhoea). Alternatively, urethritis is confirmed on the spun sediment of a first-void urine at ≥10 polymorphs/high-power field
  • Urethral swab for CULTURE if gonorrhoea is suspected or diplococci are seen — taken before antibiotics, because culture is the only way to get antimicrobial susceptibilities, and ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhoea is emerging
  • Full STI screen (HIV, syphilis)
For every M. genitalium-positive sample: test for MACROLIDE RESISTANCE, and perform a TEST OF CURE at least 5 weeks after starting treatment — resistance is common and rising, and testing earlier risks a false positive from residual nucleic acid.
Management (BASHH)
📷 Image placeholder — NGU treatment algorithm — doxycycline first-line → persistent/recurrent arms (extended azithromycin or moxifloxacin ± metronidazole) → M. genitalium resistance-guided pathway.
🟢 Uncomplicated, first-presentation NGU
  • First-line: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (preferred over azithromycin — more effective vs M. genitalium and, crucially, does NOT induce macrolide resistance). Warn about photosensitivity
  • Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding — use azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg OD for 2 days instead (BNF)
  • Alternatives: azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2 days (extended — single-dose drives resistance, so avoided); ofloxacin 200 mg BD (or 400 mg OD) 7 days
🔁 Recurrent / persistent NGU
  • First reconfirm urethritis on microscopy, exclude reinfection, poor adherence and an untreated partner, and send a first-void urine NAAT for M. genitalium with macrolide-resistance testing — the result directs treatment
  • If first-line was doxycycline → azithromycin (1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2) + metronidazole 400 mg BD 5 days
  • If first-line was azithromycin → moxifloxacin 400 mg OD 10 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD 5 days, OR doxycycline + metronidazole
  • (Metronidazole covers Trichomonas/anaerobes; moxifloxacin covers macrolide-resistant M. genitalium)
Confirmed M. genitalium: give a doxycycline 100 mg BD 7-day lead-in first in both cases (it reduces organism load), then — macrolide-sensitive → azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg OD for 2 days; macrolide-resistant → moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 7 days. Always test of cure at 5 weeks.
Fluoroquinolone caution (MHRA): moxifloxacin and ofloxacin may only be prescribed when other antibiotics are inappropriate. Counsel about tendinitis and tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm and dissection, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects, and tell the patient to stop the drug and seek advice at the first sign of tendon pain.
General advice: no sex — including oral — until treatment is complete (+ 7 days after, and until partners are treated). GUM referral, partner notification with a 4-week look-back in symptomatic men, full STI screen.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Dysuria ± urethral discharge (often asymptomatic); split into gonococcal vs non-gonococcal (NGU/NSU).
NGU causes
Chlamydia (commonest), M. genitalium (2nd, resistance issue); Ureaplasma only inconsistently; also trich/HSV/adenovirus. Many are idiopathic.
M. genitalium spectrum
Also causes epididymitis, cervicitis, endometritis, PID, reactive arthritis, tubal infertility, preterm birth.
Diagnose
NAAT (first-void urine men / vulvovaginal swab women) + urethral smear (≥5 PMNs/hpf; diplococci → gonorrhoea).
M. genitalium testing
Test every positive for MACROLIDE RESISTANCE + do a TEST OF CURE at 5 weeks from the start of treatment.
1st-line NGU
Doxycycline 100 mg BD 7 days (better vs M. genitalium, doesn’t drive resistance).
Recurrent
Reconfirm urethritis and re-test for M. genitalium with resistance first; add metronidazole 400 mg BD 5 days; moxifloxacin for macrolide-resistant M. genitalium — a fluoroquinolone, so only when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA).
Advice
GUM referral + partner notification + no sex until treated.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis:
What & Why

Syphilis is an STI caused by the spirochaete Treponema pallidum. It’s “the great imitator” — progressing through distinct stages over years, each with different (often deceptive) features; untreated it causes devastating late complications (neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis) and congenital syphilis. Rates have risen sharply in the UK.

The organism: a spirochaete (spiral-shaped bacterium), mainly an STI. Incubation ~21 days (range 9–90) to the primary lesion. Transmission: oral/vaginal/anal sex (contact with an infectious lesion), vertical (→ congenital syphilis); rarely blood-borne (transfusion of fresh infected blood). Injecting drug use and chemsex are associated risk contexts rather than separate routes.
The Decisive Fork — Which Stage?
📷 Image placeholder — Staging timeline — primary chancre (~3 wks) → secondary (~6–12 wks, range ~4 wks to 6 months) → latent (early <2 yr / late >2 yr) → tertiary (years), with the key exam feature of each stage.
1️⃣ Primary
  • Chancre — a PAINLESS, indurated genital ulcer at inoculation (highly infectious)
  • Local painless lymphadenopathy; heals spontaneously → often missed
2️⃣ Secondary (~6–12 wks)
  • A systemic, disseminated stage
  • Maculopapular rash on TRUNK, PALMS + SOLES
  • Condylomata lata (moist grey wart-like plaques), snail-track mouth ulcers, fever, lymphadenopathy, patchy alopecia
3️⃣ Latent
  • Asymptomatic — infection persists (positive serology, no signs)
  • Early latent (<2 years — potentially infectious) vs late latent (>2 years — non-infectious sexually, but can transmit vertically)
4️⃣ Tertiary (years later, ~⅓ untreated)
  • Gummas — granulomatous destructive lesions (skin, bone, organs)
  • Cardiovascular — aortitis → thoracic aortic aneurysm (ascending aorta), aortic regurgitation
  • Neurosyphilis (see below)
Exam contrast: syphilitic chancre = PAINLESS; chancroid (H. ducreyi) + herpes = painful. A painless genital ulcer → think syphilis.
Neurosyphilis & Congenital Syphilis
🧠 Neurosyphilis (can occur at ANY stage)
  • Headache, altered behaviour, dementia (general paresis)
  • Tabes dorsalis — dorsal column degeneration → sensory ataxia, lightning pains, loss of proprioception
  • Ocular syphilis (uveitis, reduced vision) and otosyphilis (sudden hearing loss, tinnitus) — sight- and hearing-threatening: refer for same-day specialist assessment and treat with the neurosyphilis regimen. Also cranial nerve palsies
  • Argyll-Robertson pupil — small, irregular pupil that ACCOMMODATES but does NOT REACT to light
👶 Congenital syphilis
  • Early (first weeks): snuffles/rhinitis, rash often involving palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, bone changes with pseudoparalysis
  • Late (from about 5–10 years): Hutchinson’s teeth (notched, peg-shaped permanent incisors)
  • Rhagades, interstitial keratitis, sabre shins, saddle nose, sensorineural deafness
  • Hutchinson’s triad = teeth + keratitis + deafness
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Serology interpretation grid — treponemal (EIA/TPPA, positive for life) vs non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL titre) across active, treated, reinfection and biological-false-positive scenarios.
Direct detection (from a lesion): dark-field microscopy + PCR of a swab from a chancre/lesion — detects T. pallidum directly (it can’t be routinely cultured).
Serology — a two-tier system
🧪 Treponemal (specific — confirm exposure)
  • EIA/CLIA (usual screen), TPHA/TPPA
  • Stay positive for life even after cure → confirm infection but can’t distinguish active from treated
📉 Non-treponemal (RPR / VDRL)
  • Sensitive but non-specific; quantitative (titres)
  • Reflect disease activity: titre falls with successful treatment, rises with active/reinfection → used to monitor response
  • Can give false positives (pregnancy, SLE/antiphospholipid, other infections) → always confirmed with a treponemal test
Neurosyphilis: lumbar puncture (CSF for VDRL, protein, cells).
Two serology traps. Prozone phenomenon: a very high antibody level can block the reaction and give a falsely NEGATIVE undiluted RPR/VDRL — classically in secondary syphilis and in pregnancy; if suspicion is high, ask the laboratory to dilute the sample. Early primary syphilis: a negative screen does not exclude incubating or very early infection — antibodies take weeks to appear, so if a chancre is present test the lesion directly (PCR/dark-field) and repeat serology at about 6 and 12 weeks after the exposure.
Follow-up: review clinically and serologically at 3, 6 and 12 months. A fourfold (two-dilution) fall in RPR/VDRL — e.g. 1:32 to 1:8 — indicates an adequate response; a fourfold rise indicates reinfection or treatment failure and prompts reassessment and re-treatment.
Management (BASHH)
Penicillin is first-line at EVERY stage — the drug of choice, reconstituted with lidocaine to reduce injection pain. The formulation differs by site of disease: depot benzathine IM for non-neurological disease, procaine or IV benzylpenicillin for neurosyphilis.
  • Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent): benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM as a single dose
  • Late latent / tertiary (non-neuro): benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses (longer — the organism divides slowly)
  • Neurosyphilis (including ocular and otological): procaine penicillin IM daily with oral probenecid for 14 days, or IV benzylpenicillin for 14 days, plus steroid cover started before the first antibiotic dose. Benzathine benzylpenicillin must NOT be used — it does not reach treponemocidal levels in the CSF
  • Penicillin allergy / alternative: doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days (28 days if late); ceftriaxone is an alternative. Macrolides no longer recommended (resistance). In pregnancy, penicillin is essential → desensitise if allergic (doxycycline contraindicated)
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: an acute febrile reaction within hours of the first antibiotic dose — fever, rash, tachycardia, headache, myalgia — from cytokine release as spirochaetes are killed en masse. Self-limiting → antipyretics (it is NOT an allergy). In pregnancy it may trigger uterine contractions and fetal distress — warn the woman, give antipyretics and fluids and monitor the fetus, but do not delay treatment; steroids are NOT recommended to prevent it in pregnancy. In neuro or cardiovascular syphilis the reaction can worsen the condition, so steroid cover IS given, started before the first antibiotic dose.
General: GUM referral, partner notification/contact tracing, full STI screen (including HIV — co-infection common). Abstain from sex until any lesions have healed and at least 2 weeks after treatment is completed, and until partners have been treated. Look-back by stage: primary — 3 months plus the duration of symptoms; secondary and early latent — 2 years; late syphilis — assess long-term partners and any children. Prevention of congenital syphilis: in the UK all pregnant women are offered syphilis serology at booking (UKHSA); a positive result triggers specialist referral and penicillin treatment, with re-testing later in pregnancy if there is ongoing risk or a change of partner.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Treponema pallidum (spirochaete); “the great imitator”; incubation ~21 days.
Primary
PAINLESS chancre + painless local nodes (vs painful herpes/chancroid).
Secondary (6–12 wks)
Rash on TRUNK + PALMS + SOLES, condylomata lata, snail-track mouth ulcers, systemic symptoms.
Latent / tertiary
Latent = asymptomatic, positive serology (early <2 yrs / late >2 yrs). Tertiary = gummas, cardiovascular (aortic aneurysm/aortitis), neurosyphilis.
Neurosyphilis
Tabes dorsalis, general paresis/dementia, ARGYLL-ROBERTSON PUPIL (accommodates but doesn’t react).
Congenital
Early: snuffles, palm/sole rash, hepatosplenomegaly. Late (from ~5–10 yrs): Hutchinson’s teeth, rhagades, keratitis, sabre shins, saddle nose, deafness. Prevented by antenatal screening at booking.
Diagnosis
Dark-field microscopy/PCR of lesion; serology = treponemal (EIA/TPPA, positive for life) + non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL, titres track activity/treatment).
Treatment
PENICILLIN at every stage (benzathine benzylpenicillin single dose early; 3 weekly doses late; procaine/IV for neuro — benzathine does NOT treat neurosyphilis). Doxycycline if allergic (not in pregnancy).
Jarisch-Herxheimer
Fever/rash/tachycardia hours after first dose → antipyretics.
